[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 5.8 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"621f45","wall_time_seconds":0.6240964,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3477,"output":"---\\r\\nname: site-teardown\\r\\ndescription: \\"Reverse engineer any website into a complete build blueprint. Analyzes the HTML structure, fetches and extracts all animation/interaction code from the site\'s JavaScript, and pulls the complete design system from the CSS. Outputs a structured teardown document with tech stack, every visual effect and how it\'s implemented, design tokens, assets needed, and a section-by-section build plan. Use this skill whenever the user wants to analyze how a website was built, reverse engineer a site, clone or recreate a website, understand what tech stack or animations a site uses, do a site teardown, deconstruct a page, figure out how an effect works on a website, or says things like \'steal this website\', \'break down this site\', \'how did they build this\', \'website blueprint\', \'analyze this site for me\', or gives you a URL and asks you to figure out how it works. Also trigger when the user pastes raw HTML source code and asks what\'s going on or how to recreate it.\\"\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Site Teardown\\r\\n\\r\\nReverse engineer any website into a complete build blueprint — tech stack, every visual effect with implementation details, full design system, and a section-by-section build plan. The output should be thorough enough that someone could hand it to Codex in a fresh session and build a clone without ever visiting the original site.\\r\\n\\r\\n## When This Skill Activates\\r\\n\\r\\n**Activate when the user wants to:**\\r\\n- Analyze how a website was built\\r\\n- Reverse engineer or deconstruct a site\\r\\n- Clone or recreate a website\'s design and animations\\r\\n- Understand what tech stack, libraries, or animation techniques a site uses\\r\\n- Get a build blueprint for a website they want to recreate\\r\\n- Understand how a specific effect on a website works (and the site hasn\'t been analyzed yet)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Example triggers:**\\r\\n- \\"Tear down this site: https://example.com\\"\\r\\n- \\"How did they build this website?\\"\\r\\n- \\"Analyze this site for me\\"\\r\\n- \\"Reverse engineer this page\\"\\r\\n- \\"I want to steal this website\'s design\\"\\r\\n- \\"Clone this site analysis\\"\\r\\n- \\"Website blueprint for [URL]\\"\\r\\n- \\"Break down this page\\"\\r\\n- \\"Deconstruct this site\\"\\r\\n- `/site-teardown`\\r\\n- `/site-teardown [URL]`\\r\\n- User pastes raw HTML and asks how to recreate it\\r\\n\\r\\n## Pipeline\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 1 — Get the HTML\\r\\n\\r\\nThe HTML is the foundation. It tells you what\'s on the page — the elements, the classes, the structure, the image/video paths, the SVGs.\\r\\n\\r\\n**If the user pastes raw HTML source code:**\\r\\n- Use it directly. Pasted HTML is more complete than a WebFetch for large pages because WebFetch processes content through a sub-model that may summarize details.\\r\\n- Scan the HTML and extract key structural information:\\r\\n  - All section/component class names\\r\\n  - Image and video source paths\\r\\n  - SVG elements (logos, icons, decorative shapes)\\r\\n  - Form structures\\r\\n  - Navigation structure\\r\\n  - Meta tags (author, description, title)\\r\\n  - Any inline styles or inline scripts\\r\\n\\r\\n**If the user only provides a URL:**\\r\\n- Use WebFetch on the URL with this prompt: \\"Return the complete HTML structure of this page. Include all class names, element hierarchy, image/video src paths, SVG elements, meta tags, script src paths, stylesheet href paths, and any inline styles or scripts. Preserve the exact class names and data attributes. Do not summarize the structure — return as much detail as possible.\\"\\r\\n- Note to user: for the most complete analysis, they can paste the raw HTML (Ctrl+U → Ctrl+A → Ctrl+C on the page).\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 2 — Find the JS and CSS File Paths\\r\\n\\r\\nFrom the HTML, locate the main application JavaScript and CSS files. These are what contain the actual behavior and styling.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Look for:**\\r\\n```html\\r\\n<!-- CSS - usually in <head> -->\\r\\n<link rel=\\"stylesheet\\" href=\\"/path/to/main.css\\">\\r\\n\\r\\n<!-- JS - usually before </body> -->\\r\\n<script src=\\"/path/to/main.js\\"></script>\\r\\n<script type=\\"module\\" src=\\"/dist/assets/app.js\\"></script>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Filter out third-party scripts** — skip these, they\'re not the site\'s custom code:\\r\\n- Google Tag Manager, Google Analytics, gtag\\r\\n- Cookie consent (iubenda, OneTrust, CookieBot)\\r\\n- reCAPTCHA, hCaptcha\\r\\n- CDN-hosted libraries (cdnjs, unpkg, jsdelivr) — note what libraries they use but don\'t fetch them\\r\\n- Social media widgets, chat widgets\\r\\n- WordPress core scripts (`/wp-includes/js/`)\\r\\n\\r\\n**Keep the main application files** — these are what you want:\\r\\n- Files from `/dist/`, `/build/`, `/assets/`, `/static/`\\r\\n- Files with names like `main.js`, `app.js`, `bundle.js`, `index.js`\\r\\n- Same pattern for CSS: `main.css`, `app.css`, `style.css`, `styles.css`\\r\\n- Modulepreload hints also point to important files: `<link rel=\\"modulepreload\\" href=\\"...\\">`\\r\\n\\r\\nConstruct the full URLs by combining the site\'s domain with the file paths.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 3 — Fetch the JavaScript\\r\\n\\r\\nUse WebFetch on the main JS file. The goal is to extract every interaction, animation, and behavior on the site.\\r\\n\\r\\nBuild the prompt dynamically using class names found in the HTML. Start with this base prompt and append the site-specific class names:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Base prompt:**\\r\\n```\\r\\nExtract ALL animation code, event listeners, scroll effects, mouse interactions,\\r\\nclick handlers, and GSAP/animation library usage from this JavaScript file.\\r\\n\\r\\nInclude:\\r\\n- Every function that manipulates the DOM, changes styles, or responds to user input\\r\\n- All ScrollTrigger/scroll-based animation configurations\\r\\n- All timeline definitions and animation sequences\\r\\n- All mousemove/mouseenter/mouseleave/click/touch handlers\\r\\n- All class toggling and DOM manipulation\\r\\n- All IntersectionObserver usage\\r\\n- All CSS custom property manipulation\\r\\n- All Lenis/locomotive/smooth scroll configurations\\r\\n- All Barba.js/Swup/page transition code\\r\\n- All slider/carousel/draggable configurations\\r\\n- All parallax implementations\\r\\n- All image sequence/frame animation logic\\r\\n- All cursor/pointer customization\\r\\n- All preloader/loading animations\\r\\n- All lazy loading logic\\r\\n- All form interaction handlers\\r\\n- All accordion/toggle/menu animations\\r\\n- Custom easing functions and timing values\\r\\n\\r\\nAlso look for any code targeting these class names from the HTML:\\r\\n[INSERT COMMA-SEPARATED LIST OF KEY CLASS NAMES FROM THE HTML]\\r\\n\\r\\nReturn actual code snippets with context about what elements they target.\\r\\nDo not summarize — return as much raw code as possible.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nReplace the class name placeholder with real classes extracted from the HTML in Step 1. Focus on classes that suggest interactivity — things with words like: hero, animate, scroll, slide, reveal, split, parallax, hover, active, open, toggle, frame, moon, star, video, zoom, marquee, cursor, loader, transition, etc.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 4 — Fetch the CSS\\r\\n\\r\\nUse WebFetch on the main CSS file. The goal is to extract the complete design system.\\r\\n\\r\\nAgain, build the prompt dynamically using actual class names from the HTML:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Base prompt:**\\r\\n```\\r\\nExtract the COMPLETE design system from this CSS file:\\r\\n\\r\\nInclude:\\r\\n- Every color value (hex, rgb, hsl, CSS custom properties)\\r\\n- Every @font-face declaration with font-family names, src paths, weights, and styles\\r\\n- Every font-family assignment and which elements use them\\r\\n- Every @keyframes animation with full keyframe definitions\\r\\n- Every CSS custom property (--variable) definition and usage\\r\\n- Every media query breakpoint and what changes at each\\r\\n- All transform and transition properties\\r\\n- All position:fixed and position:sticky elements\\r\\n- All z-index values and stacking context\\r\\n- The spacing/sizing system (padding, margin, gap patterns)\\r\\n- Border-radius values used across the site\\r\\n- Box-shadow and text-shadow values\\r\\n- Gradient definitions\\r\\n- Mix-blend-mode and filter usage\\r\\n- The responsive typography system (font sizes at different breakpoints)\\r\\n- Any CSS animations or transitions on pseudo-elements (::before, ::after)\\r\\n- Grid and flexbox layout patterns for major sections\\r\\n- Any mask-image or clip-path usage\\r\\n- The noise/grain/texture overlay implementation if present\\r\\n\\r\\nAlso extract all CSS rules for classes containing these terms:\\r\\n[INSERT COMMA-SEPARATED LIST OF KEY CLASS NAME STEMS FROM THE HTML]\\r\\n\\r\\nReturn actual CSS rules and values. Do not summarize — return as much raw CSS as possible.\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nReplace the class name placeholder with stems extracted from the HTML. For example, if the HTML has `.home-hero__moon-inner`, include `hero`, `moon`. If it has `.circle-slider__wheel`, include `circle`, `slider`, `wheel`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 5 — Assemble the Teardown Document\\r\\n\\r\\nCombine findings from all three sources (HTML, JS, CSS) into a structured markdown file.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Save to:** The user\'s working directory at `research/YYYY-MM-DD-{site-slug}-teardown.md`\\r\\n\\r\\nIf the working directory doesn\'t have a `research/` folder, save to the current directory instead.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Use this template:**\\r\\n\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n# Site Teardown: {Site Name}\\r\\n\\r\\n**URL:** {url}\\r\\n**Built by:** {agency/developer if identifiable from meta tags or footer}\\r\\n**Platform:** {WordPress/Next.js/custom/etc — inferred from HTML structure}\\r\\n**Date analyzed:** {YYYY-MM-DD}\\r\\n\\r\\n## Tech Stack (Confirmed from Source)\\r\\n\\r\\n| Technology | Evidence | Purpose |\\r\\n|---|---|---|\\r\\n| {library} | {where you saw it — script tag, code reference, etc.} | {what it does on this site} |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Design System\\r\\n\\r\\n### Colors\\r\\n| Name/Usage | Value |\\r\\n|---|---|\\r\\n| {Primary background} | {#hex} |\\r\\n\\r\\n### Typography\\r\\n| Role | Font Family | Weight | Letter-spacing | Sizes |\\r\\n|---|---|---|---|---|\\r\\n| {Headings} | {font name} | {weight} | {spacing} | {size range} |\\r\\n\\r\\nFont files: {list actual font file paths if found in @font-face}\\r\\n\\r\\n### Spacing System\\r\\n{Describe the spacing approach — CSS custom properties, fluid sizing with min()/clamp(), fixed values, etc.}\\r\\n\\r\\n### Responsive Approach\\r\\n{Media query strategy — breakpoints, orientation-based, container queries, etc.}\\r\\n\\r\\n## Effects Breakdown\\r\\n\\r\\n| Effect | Implementation | Complexity | Cloneable? |\\r\\n|---|---|---|---|\\r\\n| {effect name} | {how it works — 1-2 sentences} | {Low/Med/High} | {Yes/Partially/Hard} |\\r\\n\\r\\n## Implementation Details\\r\\n\\r\\n### {Most Impressive Effect #1}\\r\\n```\\r\\n{Detailed explanation of how it works}\\r\\n{Code snippets from the JS/CSS fetch}\\r\\n{The key insight that makes it work}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### {Most Impressive Effect #2}\\r\\n```\\r\\n{Same structure}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n{Repeat for each major effect worth detailing}\\r\\n\\r\\n## Assets Needed to Recreate\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **{Asset type}** — {description, suggested source (Midjourney prompt, stock site, generate with code, etc.)}\\r\\n\\r\\n## Build Plan\\r\\n\\r\\n### Recommended Stack\\r\\n- {Framework}: {why}\\r\\n- {Styling}: {why}\\r\\n- {Animation library}: {why}\\r\\n- {Other packages}: {why}\\r\\n\\r\\n### NPM Packages\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nnpm install {package1} {package2} {package3}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Section-by-Section Build Order\\r\\n\\r\\n**Section 1: {name}**\\r\\n- {what it contains}\\r\\n- {key interactions/animations}\\r\\n- {implementation approach}\\r\\n\\r\\n**Section 2: {name}**\\r\\n- {same structure}\\r\\n\\r\\n{Continue for all sections}\\r\\n\\r\\n## Notes\\r\\n- {Any gotchas, premium plugins needed, licensing concerns}\\r\\n- {Things that can\'t be cloned easily and suggested alternatives}\\r\\n- {Performance considerations}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Filling the Template — Guidance\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen assembling the teardown, keep these principles in mind:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Be specific, not vague.** \\"GSAP ScrollTrigger with scrub:true pinned to .hero, scaling from 1 to 0.3\\" is useful. \\"Uses scroll animations\\" is not. The person reading this needs to build it without seeing the original site.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Include the \\"reveal\\" for each effect.** The most valuable part of a teardown is showing that an impressive-looking effect has a simple implementation. If the moon illumination is just 54 images swapped on mousemove, say that clearly. If the parallax is just `translateX(mouseX / 50)`, include that formula.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Distinguish confirmed vs inferred.** If you found the exact GSAP config in the JS, say \\"confirmed from source.\\" If you\'re inferring from HTML class names and general patterns, say \\"inferred\\" so the builder knows what\'s solid and what might need adjustment.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Group effects by section.** The effects table gives the overview, but the implementation details should follow the page flow top-to-bottom so the builder can work section by section.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Be practical about assets.** Don\'t just say \\"needs images.\\" Say how many, what kind, suggest Midjourney prompts or stock photo search terms, and note if any can be generated with code (SVGs, noise textures, gradients).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Common Patterns to Watch For\\r\\n\\r\\nThese are the most common \\"impressive-looking but simple\\" patterns found on award-winning sites:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **Image sequences on scroll/mouse** — Preloaded frames, swap visibility based on input. Looks like video/3D, it\'s just images.\\r\\n- **SplitText character reveals** — GSAP SplitText wraps each character in a span, then staggers their opacity/transform.\\r\\n- **Parallax layers** — Multiple elements moving at different speeds on mousemove or scroll. Just different multipliers on transform.\\r\\n- **Scroll-scrubbed animations** — GSAP ScrollTrigger with `scrub: true`. Ties any animation to scroll position.\\r\\n- **CSS custom property animations** — JS updates a `--progress` variable, CSS uses `calc()` with it. Clean separation of behavior and style.\\r\\n- **Smooth scrolling** — Lenis or Locomotive Scroll wrapping the page. Just a library init.\\r\\n- **Page transitions** — Barba.js or Swup. Overlay fades in, content swaps, overlay fades out.\\r\\n- **Noise/grain overlay** — A fixed div with a noise texture image and `mix-blend-mode: overlay`.\\r\\n- **Custom cursors** — GSAP `quickSetter` tracking mouse position on a fixed element.\\r\\n- **Marquee text** — CSS or GSAP infinite horizontal translation loop.\\r\\n- **Magnetic buttons** — Element subtly follows cursor when hovering nearby. Just mousemove + transform on the button.\\r\\n- **Reveal on scroll** — IntersectionObserver or ScrollTrigger adding a class, CSS handles the transition.\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 5.4 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"b5045a","wall_time_seconds":0.517838,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3687,"output":"---\\r\\nname: skill-creator\\r\\ndescription: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill\'s description for better triggering accuracy.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Skill Creator\\r\\n\\r\\nA skill for creating new skills and iteratively improving them.\\r\\n\\r\\nAt a high level, the process of creating a skill goes like this:\\r\\n\\r\\n- Decide what you want the skill to do and roughly how it should do it\\r\\n- Write a draft of the skill\\r\\n- Create a few test prompts and run Codex-with-access-to-the-skill on them\\r\\n- Help the user evaluate the results both qualitatively and quantitatively\\r\\n  - While the runs happen in the background, draft some quantitative evals if there aren\'t any (if there are some, you can either use as is or modify if you feel something needs to change about them). Then explain them to the user (or if they already existed, explain the ones that already exist)\\r\\n  - Use the `eval-viewer/generate_review.py` script to show the user the results for them to look at, and also let them look at the quantitative metrics\\r\\n- Rewrite the skill based on feedback from the user\'s evaluation of the results (and also if there are any glaring flaws that become apparent from the quantitative benchmarks)\\r\\n- Repeat until you\'re satisfied\\r\\n- Expand the test set and try again at larger scale\\r\\n\\r\\nYour job when using this skill is to figure out where the user is in this process and then jump in and help them progress through these stages. So for instance, maybe they\'re like \\"I want to make a skill for X\\". You can help narrow down what they mean, write a draft, write the test cases, figure out how they want to evaluate, run all the prompts, and repeat.\\r\\n\\r\\nOn the other hand, maybe they already have a draft of the skill. In this case you can go straight to the eval/iterate part of the loop.\\r\\n\\r\\nOf course, you should always be flexible and if the user is like \\"I don\'t need to run a bunch of evaluations, just vibe with me\\", you can do that instead.\\r\\n\\r\\nThen after the skill is done (but again, the order is flexible), you can also run the skill description improver, which we have a whole separate script for, to optimize the triggering of the skill.\\r\\n\\r\\nCool? Cool.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Communicating with the user\\r\\n\\r\\nThe skill creator is liable to be used by people across a wide range of familiarity with coding jargon. If you haven\'t heard (and how could you, it\'s only very recently that it started), there\'s a trend now where the power of Codex is inspiring plumbers to open up their terminals, parents and grandparents to google \\"how to install npm\\". On the other hand, the bulk of users are probably fairly computer-literate.\\r\\n\\r\\nSo please pay attention to context cues to understand how to phrase your communication! In the default case, just to give you some idea:\\r\\n\\r\\n- \\"evaluation\\" and \\"benchmark\\" are borderline, but OK\\r\\n- for \\"JSON\\" and \\"assertion\\" you want to see serious cues from the user that they know what those things are before using them without explaining them\\r\\n\\r\\nIt\'s OK to briefly explain terms if you\'re in doubt, and feel free to clarify terms with a short definition if you\'re unsure if the user will get it.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Creating a skill\\r\\n\\r\\n### Capture Intent\\r\\n\\r\\nStart by understanding the user\'s intent. The current conversation might already contain a workflow the user wants to capture (e.g., they say \\"turn this into a skill\\"). If so, extract answers from the conversation history first — the tools used, the sequence of steps, corrections the user made, input/output formats observed. The user may need to fill the gaps, and should confirm before proceeding to the next step.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. What should this skill enable Codex to do?\\r\\n2. When should this skill trigger? (what user phrases/contexts)\\r\\n3. What\'s the expected output format?\\r\\n4. Should we set up test cases to verify the skill works? Skills with objectively verifiable outputs (file transforms, data extraction, code generation, fixed workflow steps) benefit from test cases. Skills with subjective outputs (writing style, art) often don\'t need them. Suggest the appropriate default based on the skill type, but let the user decide.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Interview and Research\\r\\n\\r\\nProactively ask questions about edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies. Wait to write test prompts until you\'ve got this part ironed out.\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck available MCPs - if useful for research (searching docs, finding similar skills, looking up best practices), research in parallel via subagents if available, otherwise inline. Come prepared with context to reduce burden on the user.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Write the SKILL.md\\r\\n\\r\\nBased on the user interview, fill in these components:\\r\\n\\r\\n- **name**: Skill identifier\\r\\n- **description**: When to trigger, what it does. This is the primary triggering mechanism - include both what the skill does AND specific contexts for when to use it. All \\"when to use\\" info goes here, not in the body. Note: currently Codex has a tendency to \\"undertrigger\\" skills -- to not use them when they\'d be useful. To combat this, please make the skill descriptions a little bit \\"pushy\\". So for instance, instead of \\"How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data.\\", you might write \\"How to build a simple fast dashboard to display internal Anthropic data. Make sure to use this skill whenever the user mentions dashboards, data visualization, internal metrics, or wants to display any kind of company data, even if they don\'t explicitly ask for a \'dashboard.\'\\"\\r\\n- **compatibility**: Required tools, dependencies (optional, rarely needed)\\r\\n- **the rest of the skill :)**\\r\\n\\r\\n### Skill Writing Guide\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Anatomy of a Skill\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nskill-name/\\r\\n├── SKILL.md (required)\\r\\n│   ├── YAML frontmatter (name, description required)\\r\\n│   └── Markdown instructions\\r\\n└── Bundled Resources (optional)\\r\\n    ├── scripts/    - Executable code for deterministic/repetitive tasks\\r\\n    ├── references/ - Docs loaded into context as needed\\r\\n    └── assets/     - Files used in output (templates, icons, fonts)\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Progressive Disclosure\\r\\n\\r\\nSkills use a three-level loading system:\\r\\n1. **Metadata** (name + description) - Always in context (~100 words)\\r\\n2. **SKILL.md body** - In context whenever skill triggers (<500 lines ideal)\\r\\n3. **Bundled resources** - As needed (unlimited, scripts can execute without loading)\\r\\n\\r\\nThese word counts are approximate and you can feel free to go longer if needed.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Key patterns:**\\r\\n- Keep SKILL.md under 500 lines; if you\'re approaching this limit, add an additional layer of hierarchy along with clear pointers about where the model using the skill should go next to follow up.\\r\\n- Reference files clearly from SKILL.md with guidance on when to read them\\r\\n- For large reference files (>300 lines), include a table of contents\\r\\n\\r\\n**Domain organization**: When a skill supports multiple domains/frameworks, organize by variant:\\r\\n```\\r\\ncloud-deploy/\\r\\n├── SKILL.md (workflow + selection)\\r\\n└── references/\\r\\n    ├── aws.md\\r\\n    ├── gcp.md\\r\\n    └── azure.md\\r\\n```\\r\\nCodex reads only the relevant reference file.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Principle of Lack of Surprise\\r\\n\\r\\nThis goes without saying, but skills must not contain malware, exploit code, or any content that could compromise system security. A skill\'s contents should not surprise the user in their intent if described. Don\'t go along with requests to create misleading skills or skills designed to facilitate unauthorized access, data exfiltration, or other malicious activities. Things like a \\"roleplay as an XYZ\\" are OK though.\\r\\n\\r\\n#### Writing Patterns\\r\\n\\r\\nPrefer using the imperative form in instructions.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Defining output formats** - You can do it like this:\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n## Report structure\\r\\nALWAYS use this exact template:\\r\\n# [Title]\\r\\n## Executive summary\\r\\n## Key findings\\r\\n## Recommendations\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Examples pattern** - It\'s useful to include examples. You can format them like this (but if \\"Input\\" and \\"Output\\" are in the examples you might want to deviate a little):\\r\\n```markdown\\r\\n## Commit message format\\r\\n**Example 1:**\\r\\nInput: Added user authentication with JWT tokens\\r\\nOutput: feat(auth): implement JWT-based authentication\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Writing Style\\r\\n\\r\\nTry to explain to the model why things are important in lieu of heavy-handed musty MUSTs. Use theory of mind and try to make the skill general and not super-narrow to specific examples. Start by writing a draft and then look at it with fresh eyes and improve it.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Test Cases\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter writing the skill draft, come up with 2-3 realistic test prompts — the kind of thing a real user would actually say. Share them with the user: [you don\'t have to use this exact language] \\"Here are a few test cases I\'d like to try. Do these look right, or do you want to add more?\\" Then run them.\\r\\n\\r\\nSave test cases to `evals/evals.json`. Don\'t write assertions yet — just the prompts. You\'ll draft assertions in the next step while the runs are in progress.\\r\\n\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \\"skill_name\\": \\"example-skill\\",\\r\\n  \\"evals\\": [\\r\\n    {\\r\\n      \\"id\\": 1,\\r\\n      \\"prompt\\": \\"User\'s task prompt\\",\\r\\n      \\"expected_output\\": \\"Description of expected result\\",\\r\\n      \\"files\\": []\\r\\n    }\\r\\n  ]\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nSee `references/schemas.md` for the full schema (including the `assertions` field, which you\'ll add later).\\r\\n\\r\\n## Running and evaluating test cases\\r\\n\\r\\nThis section is one continuous sequence — don\'t stop partway through. Do NOT use `/skill-test` or any other testing skill.\\r\\n\\r\\nPut results in `<skill-name>-workspace/` as a sibling to the skill directory. Within the workspace, organize results by iteration (`iteration-1/`, `iteration-2/`, etc.) and within that, each test case gets a directory (`eval-0/`, `eval-1/`, etc.). Don\'t create all of this upfront — just create directories as you go.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 1: Spawn all runs (with-skill AND baseline) in the same turn\\r\\n\\r\\nFor each test case, spawn two subagents in the same turn — one with the skill, one without. This is important: don\'t spawn the with-skill runs first and then come back for baselines later. Launch everything at once so it all finishes around the same time.\\r\\n\\r\\n**With-skill run:**\\r\\n\\r\\n```\\r\\nExecute this task:\\r\\n- Skill path: <path-to-skill>\\r\\n- Task: <eval prompt>\\r\\n- Input files: <eval files if any, or \\"none\\">\\r\\n- Save outputs to: <workspace>/iteration-<N>/eval-<ID>/with_skill/outputs/\\r\\n- Outputs to save: <what the user cares about — e.g., \\"the .docx file\\", \\"the final CSV\\">\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n**Baseline run** (same prompt, but the baseline depends on context):\\r\\n- **Creating a new skill**: no skill at all. Same prompt, no skill path, save to `without_skill/outputs/`.\\r\\n- **Improving an existing skill**: the old version. Before editing, snapshot the skill (`cp -r <skill-path> <workspace>/skill-snapshot/`), then point the baseline subagent at the snapshot. Save to `old_skill/outputs/`.\\r\\n\\r\\nWrite an `eval_metadata.json` for each test case (assertions can be empty for now). Give each eval a descriptive name based on what it\'s testing — not just \\"eval-0\\". Use this name for the directory too. If this iteration uses new or modified eval prompts, create these files for each new eval directory — don\'t assume they carry over from previous iterations.\\r\\n\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \\"eval_id\\": 0,\\r\\n  \\"eval_name\\": \\"descriptive-name-here\\",\\r\\n  \\"prompt\\": \\"The user\'s task prompt\\",\\r\\n  \\"assertions\\": []\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 2: While runs are in progress, draft assertions\\r\\n\\r\\nDon\'t just wait for the runs to finish — you can use this time productively. Draft quantitative assertions for each test case and explain them to the user. If assertions already exist in `evals/evals.json`, review them and explain what they check.\\r\\n\\r\\nGood assertions are objectively verifiable and have descriptive names — they should read clearly in the benchmark viewer so someone glancing at the results immediately understands what each one checks. Subjective skills (writing style, design quality) are better evaluated qualitatively — don\'t force assertions onto things that need human judgment.\\r\\n\\r\\nUpdate the `eval_metadata.json` files and `evals/evals.json` with the assertions once drafted. Also explain to the user what they\'ll see in the viewer — both the qualitative outputs and the quantitative benchmark.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 3: As runs complete, capture timing data\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen each subagent task completes, you receive a notification containing `total_tokens` and `duration_ms`. Save this data immediately to `timing.json` in the run directory:\\r\\n\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \\"total_tokens\\": 84852,\\r\\n  \\"duration_ms\\": 23332,\\r\\n  \\"total_duration_seconds\\": 23.3\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is the only opportunity to capture this data — it comes through the task notification and isn\'t persisted elsewhere. Process each notification as it arrives rather than trying to batch them.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 4: Grade, aggregate, and launch the viewer\\r\\n\\r\\nOnce all runs are done:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Grade each run** — spawn a grader subagent (or grade inline) that reads `agents/grader.md` and evaluates each assertion against the outputs. Save results to `grading.json` in each run directory. The grading.json expectations array must use the fields `text`, `passed`, and `evidence` (not `name`/`met`/`details` or other variants) — the viewer depends on these exact field names. For assertions that can be checked programmatically, write and run a script rather than eyeballing it — scripts are faster, more reliable, and can be reused across iterations.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Aggregate into benchmark** — run the aggregation script from the skill-creator directory:\\r\\n   ```bash\\r\\n   python -m scripts.aggregate_benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N --skill-name <name>\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n   This produces `benchmark.json` and `benchmark.md` with pass_rate, time, and tokens for each configuration, with mean ± stddev and the delta. If generating benchmark.json manually, see `references/schemas.md` for the exact schema the viewer expects.\\r\\nPut each with_skill version before its baseline counterpart.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Do an analyst pass** — read the benchmark data and surface patterns the aggregate stats might hide. See `agents/analyzer.md` (the \\"Analyzing Benchmark Results\\" section) for what to look for — things like assertions that always pass regardless of skill (non-discriminating), high-variance evals (possibly flaky), and time/token tradeoffs.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Launch the viewer** with both qualitative outputs and quantitative data:\\r\\n   ```bash\\r\\n   nohup python <skill-creator-path>/eval-viewer/generate_review.py \\\\\\r\\n     <workspace>/iteration-N \\\\\\r\\n     --skill-name \\"my-skill\\" \\\\\\r\\n"}'}]

[{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 7.3 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"0912c1","wall_time_seconds":0.8048524,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":4716,"output":"     --benchmark <workspace>/iteration-N/benchmark.json \\\\\\r\\n     > /dev/null 2>&1 &\\r\\n   VIEWER_PID=$!\\r\\n   ```\\r\\n   For iteration 2+, also pass `--previous-workspace <workspace>/iteration-<N-1>`.\\r\\n\\r\\n   **Cowork / headless environments:** If `webbrowser.open()` is not available or the environment has no display, use `--static <output_path>` to write a standalone HTML file instead of starting a server. Feedback will be downloaded as a `feedback.json` file when the user clicks \\"Submit All Reviews\\". After download, copy `feedback.json` into the workspace directory for the next iteration to pick up.\\r\\n\\r\\nNote: please use generate_review.py to create the viewer; there\'s no need to write custom HTML.\\r\\n\\r\\n5. **Tell the user** something like: \\"I\'ve opened the results in your browser. There are two tabs — \'Outputs\' lets you click through each test case and leave feedback, \'Benchmark\' shows the quantitative comparison. When you\'re done, come back here and let me know.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n### What the user sees in the viewer\\r\\n\\r\\nThe \\"Outputs\\" tab shows one test case at a time:\\r\\n- **Prompt**: the task that was given\\r\\n- **Output**: the files the skill produced, rendered inline where possible\\r\\n- **Previous Output** (iteration 2+): collapsed section showing last iteration\'s output\\r\\n- **Formal Grades** (if grading was run): collapsed section showing assertion pass/fail\\r\\n- **Feedback**: a textbox that auto-saves as they type\\r\\n- **Previous Feedback** (iteration 2+): their comments from last time, shown below the textbox\\r\\n\\r\\nThe \\"Benchmark\\" tab shows the stats summary: pass rates, timing, and token usage for each configuration, with per-eval breakdowns and analyst observations.\\r\\n\\r\\nNavigation is via prev/next buttons or arrow keys. When done, they click \\"Submit All Reviews\\" which saves all feedback to `feedback.json`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 5: Read the feedback\\r\\n\\r\\nWhen the user tells you they\'re done, read `feedback.json`:\\r\\n\\r\\n```json\\r\\n{\\r\\n  \\"reviews\\": [\\r\\n    {\\"run_id\\": \\"eval-0-with_skill\\", \\"feedback\\": \\"the chart is missing axis labels\\", \\"timestamp\\": \\"...\\"},\\r\\n    {\\"run_id\\": \\"eval-1-with_skill\\", \\"feedback\\": \\"\\", \\"timestamp\\": \\"...\\"},\\r\\n    {\\"run_id\\": \\"eval-2-with_skill\\", \\"feedback\\": \\"perfect, love this\\", \\"timestamp\\": \\"...\\"}\\r\\n  ],\\r\\n  \\"status\\": \\"complete\\"\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nEmpty feedback means the user thought it was fine. Focus your improvements on the test cases where the user had specific complaints.\\r\\n\\r\\nKill the viewer server when you\'re done with it:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\nkill $VIEWER_PID 2>/dev/null\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Improving the skill\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is the heart of the loop. You\'ve run the test cases, the user has reviewed the results, and now you need to make the skill better based on their feedback.\\r\\n\\r\\n### How to think about improvements\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Generalize from the feedback.** The big picture thing that\'s happening here is that we\'re trying to create skills that can be used a million times (maybe literally, maybe even more who knows) across many different prompts. Here you and the user are iterating on only a few examples over and over again because it helps move faster. The user knows these examples in and out and it\'s quick for them to assess new outputs. But if the skill you and the user are codeveloping works only for those examples, it\'s useless. Rather than put in fiddly overfitty changes, or oppressively constrictive MUSTs, if there\'s some stubborn issue, you might try branching out and using different metaphors, or recommending different patterns of working. It\'s relatively cheap to try and maybe you\'ll land on something great.\\r\\n\\r\\n2. **Keep the prompt lean.** Remove things that aren\'t pulling their weight. Make sure to read the transcripts, not just the final outputs — if it looks like the skill is making the model waste a bunch of time doing things that are unproductive, you can try getting rid of the parts of the skill that are making it do that and seeing what happens.\\r\\n\\r\\n3. **Explain the why.** Try hard to explain the **why** behind everything you\'re asking the model to do. Today\'s LLMs are *smart*. They have good theory of mind and when given a good harness can go beyond rote instructions and really make things happen. Even if the feedback from the user is terse or frustrated, try to actually understand the task and why the user is writing what they wrote, and what they actually wrote, and then transmit this understanding into the instructions. If you find yourself writing ALWAYS or NEVER in all caps, or using super rigid structures, that\'s a yellow flag — if possible, reframe and explain the reasoning so that the model understands why the thing you\'re asking for is important. That\'s a more humane, powerful, and effective approach.\\r\\n\\r\\n4. **Look for repeated work across test cases.** Read the transcripts from the test runs and notice if the subagents all independently wrote similar helper scripts or took the same multi-step approach to something. If all 3 test cases resulted in the subagent writing a `create_docx.py` or a `build_chart.py`, that\'s a strong signal the skill should bundle that script. Write it once, put it in `scripts/`, and tell the skill to use it. This saves every future invocation from reinventing the wheel.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis task is pretty important (we are trying to create billions a year in economic value here!) and your thinking time is not the blocker; take your time and really mull things over. I\'d suggest writing a draft revision and then looking at it anew and making improvements. Really do your best to get into the head of the user and understand what they want and need.\\r\\n\\r\\n### The iteration loop\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter improving the skill:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Apply your improvements to the skill\\r\\n2. Rerun all test cases into a new `iteration-<N+1>/` directory, including baseline runs. If you\'re creating a new skill, the baseline is always `without_skill` (no skill) — that stays the same across iterations. If you\'re improving an existing skill, use your judgment on what makes sense as the baseline: the original version the user came in with, or the previous iteration.\\r\\n3. Launch the reviewer with `--previous-workspace` pointing at the previous iteration\\r\\n4. Wait for the user to review and tell you they\'re done\\r\\n5. Read the new feedback, improve again, repeat\\r\\n\\r\\nKeep going until:\\r\\n- The user says they\'re happy\\r\\n- The feedback is all empty (everything looks good)\\r\\n- You\'re not making meaningful progress\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Advanced: Blind comparison\\r\\n\\r\\nFor situations where you want a more rigorous comparison between two versions of a skill (e.g., the user asks \\"is the new version actually better?\\"), there\'s a blind comparison system. Read `agents/comparator.md` and `agents/analyzer.md` for the details. The basic idea is: give two outputs to an independent agent without telling it which is which, and let it judge quality. Then analyze why the winner won.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis is optional, requires subagents, and most users won\'t need it. The human review loop is usually sufficient.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Description Optimization\\r\\n\\r\\nThe description field in SKILL.md frontmatter is the primary mechanism that determines whether Codex invokes a skill. After creating or improving a skill, offer to optimize the description for better triggering accuracy.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 1: Generate trigger eval queries\\r\\n\\r\\nCreate 20 eval queries — a mix of should-trigger and should-not-trigger. Save as JSON:\\r\\n\\r\\n```json\\r\\n[\\r\\n  {\\"query\\": \\"the user prompt\\", \\"should_trigger\\": true},\\r\\n  {\\"query\\": \\"another prompt\\", \\"should_trigger\\": false}\\r\\n]\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nThe queries must be realistic and something a Codex or Codex.ai user would actually type. Not abstract requests, but requests that are concrete and specific and have a good amount of detail. For instance, file paths, personal context about the user\'s job or situation, column names and values, company names, URLs. A little bit of backstory. Some might be in lowercase or contain abbreviations or typos or casual speech. Use a mix of different lengths, and focus on edge cases rather than making them clear-cut (the user will get a chance to sign off on them).\\r\\n\\r\\nBad: `\\"Format this data\\"`, `\\"Extract text from PDF\\"`, `\\"Create a chart\\"`\\r\\n\\r\\nGood: `\\"ok so my boss just sent me this xlsx file (its in my downloads, called something like \'Q4 sales final FINAL v2.xlsx\') and she wants me to add a column that shows the profit margin as a percentage. The revenue is in column C and costs are in column D i think\\"`\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the **should-trigger** queries (8-10), think about coverage. You want different phrasings of the same intent — some formal, some casual. Include cases where the user doesn\'t explicitly name the skill or file type but clearly needs it. Throw in some uncommon use cases and cases where this skill competes with another but should win.\\r\\n\\r\\nFor the **should-not-trigger** queries (8-10), the most valuable ones are the near-misses — queries that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something different. Think adjacent domains, ambiguous phrasing where a naive keyword match would trigger but shouldn\'t, and cases where the query touches on something the skill does but in a context where another tool is more appropriate.\\r\\n\\r\\nThe key thing to avoid: don\'t make should-not-trigger queries obviously irrelevant. \\"Write a fibonacci function\\" as a negative test for a PDF skill is too easy — it doesn\'t test anything. The negative cases should be genuinely tricky.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 2: Review with user\\r\\n\\r\\nPresent the eval set to the user for review using the HTML template:\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Read the template from `assets/eval_review.html`\\r\\n2. Replace the placeholders:\\r\\n   - `__EVAL_DATA_PLACEHOLDER__` → the JSON array of eval items (no quotes around it — it\'s a JS variable assignment)\\r\\n   - `__SKILL_NAME_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill\'s name\\r\\n   - `__SKILL_DESCRIPTION_PLACEHOLDER__` → the skill\'s current description\\r\\n3. Write to a temp file (e.g., `/tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`) and open it: `open /tmp/eval_review_<skill-name>.html`\\r\\n4. The user can edit queries, toggle should-trigger, add/remove entries, then click \\"Export Eval Set\\"\\r\\n5. The file downloads to `~/Downloads/eval_set.json` — check the Downloads folder for the most recent version in case there are multiple (e.g., `eval_set (1).json`)\\r\\n\\r\\nThis step matters — bad eval queries lead to bad descriptions.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 3: Run the optimization loop\\r\\n\\r\\nTell the user: \\"This will take some time — I\'ll run the optimization loop in the background and check on it periodically.\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nSave the eval set to the workspace, then run in the background:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\npython -m scripts.run_loop \\\\\\r\\n  --eval-set <path-to-trigger-eval.json> \\\\\\r\\n  --skill-path <path-to-skill> \\\\\\r\\n  --model <model-id-powering-this-session> \\\\\\r\\n  --max-iterations 5 \\\\\\r\\n  --verbose\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nUse the model ID from your system prompt (the one powering the current session) so the triggering test matches what the user actually experiences.\\r\\n\\r\\nWhile it runs, periodically tail the output to give the user updates on which iteration it\'s on and what the scores look like.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis handles the full optimization loop automatically. It splits the eval set into 60% train and 40% held-out test, evaluates the current description (running each query 3 times to get a reliable trigger rate), then calls Codex to propose improvements based on what failed. It re-evaluates each new description on both train and test, iterating up to 5 times. When it\'s done, it opens an HTML report in the browser showing the results per iteration and returns JSON with `best_description` — selected by test score rather than train score to avoid overfitting.\\r\\n\\r\\n### How skill triggering works\\r\\n\\r\\nUnderstanding the triggering mechanism helps design better eval queries. Skills appear in Codex\'s `available_skills` list with their name + description, and Codex decides whether to consult a skill based on that description. The important thing to know is that Codex only consults skills for tasks it can\'t easily handle on its own — simple, one-step queries like \\"read this PDF\\" may not trigger a skill even if the description matches perfectly, because Codex can handle them directly with basic tools. Complex, multi-step, or specialized queries reliably trigger skills when the description matches.\\r\\n\\r\\nThis means your eval queries should be substantive enough that Codex would actually benefit from consulting a skill. Simple queries like \\"read file X\\" are poor test cases — they won\'t trigger skills regardless of description quality.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Step 4: Apply the result\\r\\n\\r\\nTake `best_description` from the JSON output and update the skill\'s SKILL.md frontmatter. Show the user before/after and report the scores.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n### Package and Present (only if `present_files` tool is available)\\r\\n\\r\\nCheck whether you have access to the `present_files` tool. If you don\'t, skip this step. If you do, package the skill and present the .skill file to the user:\\r\\n\\r\\n```bash\\r\\npython -m scripts.package_skill <path/to/skill-folder>\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\nAfter packaging, direct the user to the resulting `.skill` file path so they can install it.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Codex.ai-specific instructions\\r\\n\\r\\nIn Codex.ai, the core workflow is the same (draft → test → review → improve → repeat), but because Codex.ai doesn\'t have subagents, some mechanics change. Here\'s what to adapt:\\r\\n\\r\\n**Running test cases**: No subagents means no parallel execution. For each test case, read the skill\'s SKILL.md, then follow its instructions to accomplish the test prompt yourself. Do them one at a time. This is less rigorous than independent subagents (you wrote the skill and you\'re also running it, so you have full context), but it\'s a useful sanity check — and the human review step compensates. Skip the baseline runs — just use the skill to complete the task as requested.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Reviewing results**: If you can\'t open a browser (e.g., Codex.ai\'s VM has no display, or you\'re on a remote server), skip the browser reviewer entirely. Instead, present results directly in the conversation. For each test case, show the prompt and the output. If the output is a file the user needs to see (like a .docx or .xlsx), save it to the filesystem and tell them where it is so they can download and inspect it. Ask for feedback inline: \\"How does this look? Anything you\'d change?\\"\\r\\n\\r\\n**Benchmarking**: Skip the quantitative benchmarking — it relies on baseline comparisons which aren\'t meaningful without subagents. Focus on qualitative feedback from the user.\\r\\n\\r\\n**The iteration loop**: Same as before — improve the skill, rerun the test cases, ask for feedback — just without the browser reviewer in the middle. You can still organize results into iteration directories on the filesystem if you have one.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Description optimization**: This section requires the `Codex` CLI tool (specifically `Codex -p`) which is only available in Codex. Skip it if you\'re on Codex.ai.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Blind comparison**: Requires subagents. Skip it.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Packaging**: The `package_skill.py` script works anywhere with Python and a filesystem. On Codex.ai, you can run it and the user can download the resulting `.skill` file.\\r\\n\\r\\n**Updating an existing skill**: The user might be asking you to update an existing skill, not create a new one. Copy to `/tmp/skill-name/`, edit there, and package from the copy.\\r\\n- **If packaging manually, stage in `/tmp/` first**, then copy to the output directory -- direct writes may fail due to permissions.\\r\\n\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n## Cowork-Specific Instructions\\r\\n\\r\\nIf you\'re in Cowork, the main things to know are:\\r\\n\\r\\n- You have subagents, so the main workflow (spawn test cases in parallel, run baselines, grade, etc.) all works. [{'type': 'input_text', 'text': 'Script completed\nWall time 11.9 seconds\nOutput:\n'}, {'type': 'input_text', 'text': '{"chunk_id":"65b737","wall_time_seconds":1.4110296,"exit_code":0,"original_token_count":3917,"output":"---\\r\\nname: consultation-email-assistant\\r\\ndescription: >-\\r\\n  Joshua\'s LSAT tutoring email assistant for consultation inquiries and post-consultation follow-ups. Use this\\r\\n  whenever Joshua says \\"run consultation request\\", \\"run consultation follow-up\\", or asks to reply to a tutoring\\r\\n  inquiry, draft a consultation reply, send someone the consultation/booking link, or follow up after a\\r\\n  consultation call, even if he doesn\'t name the skill. Trigger on any request to draft, personalize, or send\\r\\n  email to an LSAT prospect or student from contact@aspiringattorneys.com about booking a consultation,\\r\\n  services, rates, or next steps after a call. Drafts in Joshua\'s voice using the bundled golden templates,\\r\\n  puts the draft in Gmail, and only sends after Joshua approves.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Consultation Email Assistant\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua runs an LSAT tutoring business (aspiringattorneys.com). This skill turns two recurring email jobs into one-word commands: replying to new consultation inquiries, and following up after a consultation call. Both write drafts into Gmail in Joshua\'s voice and never send without his approval.\\r\\n\\r\\nEverything needed is bundled in `references/`, so this works in any session without depending on external workspace files. Read the relevant reference file before drafting.\\r\\n\\r\\n- `references/voice-principles.md` — how Joshua writes. Read before drafting anything.\\r\\n- `references/inquiry-reply-template.md` — the golden template for replying to new inquiries.\\r\\n- `references/followup-template.md` — the golden template for post-consultation follow-ups.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Core rules (apply to every draft)\\r\\n\\r\\n- Draft into Gmail. **Never send without Joshua\'s explicit go-ahead.** This is the whole point: he stays in control.\\r\\n- Write in his voice (see voice-principles). Prose only, no bullet points in the email body, no em dashes, under ~150 words.\\r\\n- Always personalize to what the person actually said or what came up on the call. Mirror at least one real detail (score, timeline, referral, platform, struggle, goal). A generic draft is a failure.\\r\\n- Reply inside the existing thread with that person rather than starting a new one.\\r\\n- Greeting \\"Hi [First name],\\". Sign \\"Best,\\\\nJoshua\\" unless the template says otherwise.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Command: \\"run consultation request\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nFor a new inquiry (someone asking about tutoring, rates, availability, or booking).\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Find the most recent unanswered inquiry in Gmail (`in:inbox is:unread newer_than:7d -in:sent`, newest genuine inquiry about services/rates/availability/booking). Handle just that one unless Joshua says \\"all\\". If nothing qualifies, tell him plainly rather than inventing one.\\r\\n2. Read `references/voice-principles.md` and `references/inquiry-reply-template.md`.\\r\\n3. Draft a personalized reply that addresses what they actually wrote, using the template. Include the rate line only if they asked about cost. The consultation link is the next step.\\r\\n4. Create it as a Gmail draft (reply in the existing thread).\\r\\n5. Show Joshua the draft and ask him to approve. Send only after he approves. If he wants changes, revise and ask again.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Command: \\"run consultation follow-up\\"\\r\\n\\r\\nFor after a consultation call.\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Find the most recent consultation ready for follow-up: a Google Calendar event titled \\"Consultation between Joshua and {Name}\\" that is in the past and has a \\"Notes by Gemini\\" / Transcript attachment, and to which no follow-up has been sent yet. Handle just the newest unless Joshua says \\"all\\". If none are ready, say so.\\r\\n2. Read `references/voice-principles.md` and `references/followup-template.md`.\\r\\n3. Read the Gemini notes doc (Drive) for that consultation and pull the details to mirror (current/target score, platform, timeline, struggles) and the next-steps items.\\r\\n4. Draft a personalized follow-up using the template: Variant A by default, Variant C (tiered options) if the notes show cost-sensitivity, or the onboarding note if they already booked and paid. Create it as a Gmail draft, replying in the existing thread.\\r\\n5. Show Joshua the draft, then ask him how to send it using a multiple-choice question with these options: **Send now**, **Send in 8 hours**, **Send in 16 hours** (he can also choose to keep it as a draft or edit).\\r\\n   - Send now: send after he picks it.\\r\\n   - Send in 8 / 16 hours: schedule a one-time send at that time for that specific draft, and confirm the send time back to him. (Note: a delayed send fires while the app is open; if closed at that time, it goes out on next launch.)\\r\\n   - Keep as draft / edit: leave it in drafts, revise if asked, do not send.\\r\\n\\r\\nNever send a follow-up without Joshua choosing a send option.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Why it works this way\\r\\n\\r\\nThe approval gate exists because these emails go to real prospects and personalization matters more than speed; a wrong auto-send is costly. The Gemini-notes attachment is used as the \\"the call actually happened\\" signal so follow-ups never fire on no-shows. The templates encode patterns pulled from Joshua\'s real sent mail, so drafts should sound like him out of the box, but always adapt to the specific person rather than pasting the skeleton.\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: facebook-consultation-requests\\r\\ndescription: >-\\r\\n  Joshua\'s Facebook Messenger assistant for LSAT tutoring service requests. Use this whenever Joshua says\\r\\n  \\"run facebook requests\\", \\"run messenger requests\\", \\"check my facebook messages\\", or asks to find people\\r\\n  messaging him about tutoring on Facebook/Messenger and reply to them, even if he doesn\'t name the skill.\\r\\n  Trigger on any request to pull unread Messenger conversations, find requests for his LSAT services on\\r\\n  Facebook, or draft replies to prospects who messaged him there. Reads Messenger through the Codex in\\r\\n  Chrome browser tools, finds genuine service inquiries, and drafts the consultation reply in Joshua\'s voice.\\r\\n  It types the reply into the chat but never sends without Joshua\'s explicit approval.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# Facebook Consultation Requests\\r\\n\\r\\nJoshua gets LSAT tutoring inquiries through Facebook Messenger, not just email. This skill finds the real service requests among his conversations and drafts the same consultation reply he\'d send by hand, using the browser (Facebook has no data connector, so this runs through Codex in Chrome on his logged-in Chrome).\\r\\n\\r\\nRead `references/messenger-consultation-script.md` before drafting.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Access\\r\\n\\r\\nFacebook Messenger is a JavaScript app, so plain text extraction only returns the open thread. Use the Codex in Chrome tools: navigate to Messenger, screenshot the conversation list, and read individual threads by opening them. Joshua\'s Chrome (Work profile) is already logged in.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Where requests live (check all three)\\r\\n\\r\\nNew inquiries do not reliably land in one place:\\r\\n- **Unread** tab (left rail) — but this often holds stale system items (missed calls, \\"you\'re now friends\\"), so read the actual latest message, don\'t assume unread means a new inquiry.\\r\\n- **Message requests** (the \\"...\\" menu next to Chats → Message requests → \\"You may know\\") — where strangers\' first messages go.\\r\\n- **Spam** tab within Message requests — legitimate inquiries sometimes get filtered here; skip obvious group-chat noise.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What counts as a service request\\r\\n\\r\\nA genuine request is an individual person asking about LSAT tutoring, rates, availability, booking, or help with their score/prep. Skip: group chats, system notifications, \\"left the group\\", friend-add notices, and people Joshua is already actively working with (unless they\'re asking to book again).\\r\\n\\r\\n## The workflow\\r\\n\\r\\n1. Open Messenger via Chrome and screenshot the Unread list. Then check Message requests and Spam.\\r\\n2. For each conversation that looks like a real inquiry, open it and read the person\'s message so the reply addresses what they actually said.\\r\\n3. Read `references/messenger-consultation-script.md` and write the reply in Joshua\'s voice, personalized to their message (mirror their score, timeline, or goal if mentioned). Keep it warm and short, the way he writes.\\r\\n4. **Type the reply into the message box, but do NOT press Enter/Send.** On Messenger, text left in the composer is effectively the draft. This is the safety gate.\\r\\n5. Screenshot it and show Joshua the drafted reply for that person. Ask him to approve.\\r\\n6. Only after he approves, send it (press Enter or click Send). If he wants changes, clear the box, retype, and ask again. Handle one conversation at a time unless he says \\"all\\".\\r\\n\\r\\nNever send a Messenger reply without Joshua\'s explicit approval, and never message a group chat or someone who isn\'t clearly a prospect.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Why it works this way\\r\\n\\r\\nThese messages go to real prospects and personalization matters, so the approval gate is the whole point. Facebook has no API for personal messages, so the browser is the only route, and typing-without-sending is the cleanest way to stage a reviewable draft in a chat app that has no real draft state.\\r\\n---\\r\\nname: lsat-drill-builder\\r\\ndescription: Generate a new LSAT \\"argument dissection\\" drill in the same interactive style as the First Sentence vs Rebuttal drill, for any LR topic. Use when Joshua asks to build, create, or generate a drill, a dissection lab, an argument-parts practice set, or a \\"drill like the rebuttal one\\" for a new topic (assumptions, flaws, strengthen/weaken, parallel reasoning, conclusion ID, etc.). Produces a standalone single-file HTML drill with all the same features.\\r\\n---\\r\\n\\r\\n# LSAT Drill Builder\\r\\n\\r\\nThis skill regenerates the interactive argument-dissection drill for a new topic by reusing a finished template and swapping only the content. Every interaction, animation, color rule, and scoring behavior carries over automatically because you do not rewrite the engine. You replace two data blocks.\\r\\n\\r\\n## What you are building\\r\\n\\r\\nA standalone, single-file HTML drill (no dependencies, runs offline, persists to localStorage) where a student dissects ~20 LSAT stimuli step by step: identify indicator words, select the main conclusion, classify the structure, then select the supporting/opposing parts. It ends with a session review and an interactive answer key.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The template\\r\\n\\r\\n`assets/drill-template.html` is the complete, working drill. Treat it as the engine. Do NOT touch the CSS, the JavaScript functions, the step flow, the animations, or the review/answer-key code. You only edit content.\\r\\n\\r\\n## The only two things you change\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **`const drillsData = [ ... ];`** the array of questions.\\r\\n2. **`const drillExplanations = { ... };`** the per-question coaching text.\\r\\n\\r\\nBoth are near the middle of the file. Find them by searching for `const drillsData = [` and `const drillExplanations = {`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### drillsData item shape\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\n{ id: 1, type: \'first\', parts: [\\r\\n    {id: \'p1\', text: \\"Sentence with <i-w t=\\\\\\"Opinion Indicator\\\\\\">should</i-w> tagged.\\", isC: true},\\r\\n    {id: \'p2\', text: \\"A supporting sentence.\\", isS: true},\\r\\n    {id: \'p3\', text: \\"Another supporting sentence.\\", isS: true}\\r\\n], feedback: \\"One short paragraph explaining the dissection.\\" }\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n- `id`: 1-based, sequential.\\r\\n- `type`: the structure the student must classify. Use `\'first\'` or `\'rebuttal\'` for this drill family. If a NEW topic needs different categories, see \\"Adapting the classification step\\".\\r\\n- `parts`: each sentence/clause of the stimulus, in order. Flags:\\r\\n  - `isC: true` = main conclusion (exactly one per question).\\r\\n  - `isS: true` = support / premise (zero or more).\\r\\n  - `isO: true` = opposing viewpoint (zero or more). A part can be both `isO` and `isS`.\\r\\n- `text`: the sentence. Wrap indicator words inline as `<i-w t=\\"Type\\">word</i-w>`. Escape quotes inside JS strings: `<i-w t=\\\\\\"Premise Indicator\\\\\\">because</i-w>`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### Indicator word types (the `t=\\"...\\"` values)\\r\\n\\r\\nUse exactly these so colors map correctly:\\r\\n\\r\\n- `\\"Conclusion Indicator\\"`: so, thus, hence, therefore, it follows, as a result, consequently, this shows that, conclude\\r\\n- `\\"Premise Indicator\\"`: for, after all, because, since (do NOT tag \\"and\\")\\r\\n- `\\"Pivot\\"`: but, yet, however\\r\\n- `\\"Opposing Viewpoint\\"`: some people say, it is commonly believed, some economists believe, etc.\\r\\n- `\\"Concession Indicator\\"`: although, while, despite, granted, naturally\\r\\n- `\\"Opinion Indicator\\"`: clearly, obviously, evidently, ought, must, should\\r\\n\\r\\nColors are driven by type: Premise/Support = orange, Opposing = red, Pivot = purple, Concession = grey. Don\'t invent new type strings without also adding a color in `parseIndicators`.\\r\\n\\r\\n### drillExplanations item shape\\r\\n\\r\\n```js\\r\\n1: {\\r\\n    title: \\"Short scannable title\\",\\r\\n    why_conclusion: \\"Why that sentence is the conclusion.\\",\\r\\n    why_structure: \\"Why this structure classification.\\",\\r\\n    why_follow_up: \\"Why those are the supports / opposing view.\\",\\r\\n    takeaway: \\"One or two tight sentences naming the identifying signal.\\"\\r\\n}\\r\\n```\\r\\n\\r\\n- Keys must match the `id`s in `drillsData`.\\r\\n- Write `title` and `takeaway` in Joshua\'s LSAT U voice. If the `lsat-u-voice` skill is available, use it. Voice in one line: concrete, confident, no hedging, no em dashes, a short punchy landing. The `takeaway` should point at the actual tell (the indicator word or the structural move), not vague encouragement.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Step-by-step procedure\\r\\n\\r\\n1. **Get the topic and the stimuli.** Ask Joshua which LR topic and whether he\'s providing the 20 stimuli or wants you to draft them. Never invent LSAT questions silently; confirm source.\\r\\n2. **Read `assets/drill-template.html`** so you know the exact current formatting.\\r\\n3. **Write the new `drillsData`**: tag every indicator word, set isC/isS/isO on every part, write a short `feedback` per question.\\r\\n4. **Write the new `drillExplanations`** with matching ids, in voice.\\r\\n5. **Replace only those two blocks** in a copy of the template. Leave everything else byte-for-byte.\\r\\n6. **Update the homepage title** (search for `First Sentence vs Rebuttal Drill`) and the drill context label if the topic name should change.\\r\\n7. **Verify** (see below).\\r\\n8. **Save** as `<Topic Name> (drill).html` in Joshua\'s selected folder and present it.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Adapting the classification step (only if the new topic needs it)\\r\\n\\r\\nStep 3 offers two buttons: \\"First-Sentence Conclusion\\" and \\"Rebuttal\\", validated against `type`. If the new topic classifies something else, change the two button labels in `renderDrillControls` (search for `selectStructure(\'first\')`) and the `type` values in `drillsData`. Keep the two-option pattern unless Joshua asks for more. If a topic doesn\'t need a classification step at all, ask Joshua before removing it, since it touches the step flow.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Verification (always run before delivering)\\r\\n\\r\\n- Syntax-check the inline JS: extract the `<script>` block and `new Function(it)` in Node. Must parse.\\r\\n- Every `drillExplanations` id has a matching `drillsData` id and vice versa.\\r\\n- Each question has exactly one `isC`; every `\'first\'` has at least one `isS`; every `\'rebuttal\'` has a selectable step-4 target.\\r\\n- No `<i-w>` tag wraps the word \\"and\\".\\r\\n- Walk it mentally: homepage to drill to review to answer key.\\r\\n\\r\\n## Features that must keep working\\r\\n\\r\\nIndicator-word breathing pulse (reduced-motion aware), wrong-answer shake/flash, selected-phrase glow, step feedback banners, staggered entrance animations, skeleton loaders, toasts, hover tooltip on revealed indicators, multi-select supports/opposing with lenient wrong-clicks, clean/recovered/assisted scoring, collapsed per-question breakdown, interactive answer key with clickable jump-back, Prev/Next nav, percentage-only progress, localStorage autosave, full keyboard/ARIA support. All live in the untouched engine, so they survive as long as you only edit the two data blocks.\\r\\n"}'}]
